title: On the Three Modes of Persuasion
author: Study the Great Books
summary: This piece from the Study the Great Books newsletter is a primer on classical rhetoric's three modes of persuasion - logos (appeal to intellect), pathos (appeal to emotion), and ethos (appeal to the speaker's character) - framed within the tradition running from Aristotle through Quintilian. The author argues that a skilled rhetorician must read the audience to choose which mode to emphasize, illustrating the point with a hypothetical logic lecture that needs a dose of pathos when delivered to skeptical homeschooling parents rather than a room of philosophers. Central to the argument is Quintilian's definition of the ideal orator as "a good man, skilled in speaking," which the author uses to insist that rhetorical technique is morally neutral - it becomes rhetoric in service of the Good or sophistry in service of Gain depending entirely on the character of the speaker. The piece closes with a protective argument for teaching rhetoric explicitly: those who understand nothing of persuasion's tools are the most defenseless against speakers who do, whether in advertising, news, or casual conversation.
points: The essay grounds classical rhetoric's three modes of persuasion (logos, pathos, ethos) in the claim that a skilled rhetorician chooses among them based on audience, not subject matter alone.

Quoting Quintilian's definition of the orator as 'a good man, skilled in speaking,' the piece argues rhetorical skill is morally neutral technology that becomes good or bad only in the hands of the speaker who wields it.
The core distinction drawn is between the rhetor, who persuades for the Good, and the sophist, who persuades for Gain — the same three modes serve either purpose.
The practical stakes are framed as protective: those ignorant of rhetoric's tools are the most vulnerable to being manipulated by 'unprincipled' speakers who do understand them.
quotes: Logos is the mode of persuasion that appeals to the intellect of its audience. A persuasive speech or essay that is logos heavy will rely largely on rational argumentation and be driven by data, syllogistic reasoning, and common sense argument.

Pathos is the mode of persuasion that appeals to the emotions of its audience. A persuasive speech or essay that is pathos heavy will rely largely on appeals to sympathy or anger or some other emotion.
It doesn't matter if you are right if you cannot persuade. It doesn't matter if you are a good person full of excellent knowledge if they don't trust or like you.
This well made point is why it is of critical importance for teachers of Rhetoric to not simply teach methods and modes, but to inculcate a love for what is true, good, and beautiful.

A good rhetor will not only refuse to lift a finger to persuade anyone into folly, but he will throw his whole person into the fight against it. A good rhetor desires truth for himself, wants to love and hate what he ought, is in pursuit of living the good life, and he wishes these things for his neighbor also.
Some have criticized rhetoric itself because of the abuses to which it can be put, but rhetoric doesn't abuse people, people abuse people.
But above all he must possess the quality which Cato places first and which is in the very nature of things the greatest and most important, that is, he must be a good man.
